subject: mTLS client mapping & SRV-based routing for private endpoints
messages:
From: Diego Fernandez <diego_fernandez@redwood.com>
To: Alex Monroe <amonroe@intellibank.com>
Cc: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.com>, Lauren Bishop <lauren_bishop@redwood.com>
Date: Tue, 29 Sep 2026 08:12:00 -0700
Subject: mTLS client mapping & SRV-based routing for private endpoints

Alex —

Thanks again for the walkthrough yesterday. As promised, I put together our recommended approach and a few open questions so we can converge on an operational design for your private deployment (VPC, customer-managed). High level: we want a pattern that lets you validate and map client identities reliably while still allowing flexible service variants (canary / legacy) without touching client configuration frequently.

Proposed pattern (summary):
- Use DNS SRV records to publish logical service endpoints (e.g. _redwood-api._tcp.redbank.internal) that map to host:port pairs for different runtime variants. SRV gives us the flexibility to change ports/targets without rotating client certs.
- Client authentication via mutual TLS (client certs). Map client cert identity to a tenant using one of two primary signals: SAN (URI/email/other OIDs) OR a short subject attribute pinned in our tenant mapping (preferred: SAN URI).
- Termination model: two valid options — 1) edge-proxy terminates mTLS and injects tenant header (proxy-mode), 2) end-to-end mTLS with our runtime validating client cert directly (e2e). We should choose based on your compliance needs.
- Certificate pinning: optional for higher-assurance clients. Recommend JWK/thumbprint pinning at the SDK layer for mobile/embedded clients. For server-to-server, rely on OCSP stapling + short-lived client certs.
- Rotation: issue client certs with ~90d expiry and provide automated CSR flow; support immediate revocation via CRL/OCSP.

Open questions for your team:
1) Do you prefer proxy-terminate (easier for RBAC header injection) or strict e2e (minimal network terminators)?
2) Can you publish a short list of the expected client populations and whether they can handle SRV lookups? (Some embedded devices cannot do SRV.)
3) Any requirement for pinned key material on your side (we can support either pin-by-cert or pin-by-jwk thumbprint)?

I attached a quick diagram (mTLS-mapping-diagram.pdf) showing the SRV mapping and example certificate fields. Once we get answers above I can schedule an engineering workshop to produce the final runbook.

Next steps:
- Alex: confirm SRV capability and client populations
- Diego: draft detailed mapping options + checklist
- Kimberly/Lauren: review for security/legal implications

Thanks,
Diego Fernandez
Staff Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

Diego —

This is great, thanks. A few quick answers and clarifications from our side:
- Most of our clients are backend services (Java/Go) that can handle SRV lookups. We have a small fleet of legacy devices (firmware) that only do A/AAAA + port; those will require a fallback host:port mapping.
- For compliance we prefer end-to-end mTLS for banking APIs. Proxy termination is acceptable for non-sensitive telemetry pipelines only.
- We can support SAN URI mapping for tenant id; we currently populate the URI with a tenant GUID in our cert issuance process.
- Pinning: desktop/mobile apps could accept pinning, but backend services prefer standard PKI with OCSP (less operational pain).

Attaching our network sketch (network-topology-intellibank.png) so you can see our resolver topology and where SRV would be visible.

Would appreciate a recommended fallback design for the legacy devices. Also please include the revocation playbook in the checklist you mentioned.

—Alex
Alex Monroe

From: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: mTLS client mapping & SRV-based routing for private endpoints

Team —

Thanks Diego and Alex for the context. Drafting a concise internal recommendation below so we can present a single plan to IntelliBank in the workshop. Please review and flag anything you disagree with.

Recommendation (differentiated paths):
A) Compliance-first (IntelliBank banking APIs):
  - End-to-end mTLS: rust-based runtime validates client certs directly.
  - Map tenant using SAN URI (URI contains tenant GUID).
  - Use SRV records for logical service discovery, but publish a per-tenant A/AAAA fallback record for legacy devices (low TTL, monitored).
  - Short-lived client certs (45–90 days) + OCSP stapling and active revocation check on critical paths.
  - No proxy injection of tenant headers for core banking endpoints.

B) Operational-first (telemetry/analytics):
  - Edge TLS termination in a hardened proxy (Envoy) with mTLS to clients and mTLS to origin (mutual on both sides).
  - Proxy injects tenant header after validating cert mapping. SRV routing used to steer to proxy clusters.

PKI & Pinning notes:
- Recommend pinning only for mobile/desktop clients where update rollout is manageable.
- For server-to-server, pinning creates operational risk; prefer short cert life and automated CSRs.
- If pinning is required, use JWK thumbprints and store trusted thumbprints in our tenant mapping service (not in client code).

Operational checklist (attached: client-mapping-checklist.md) includes steps for: cert issuance, CSR flow, SRV record naming convention, TTL guidance, monitoring alerts for SRV/A drift, OCSP/CRL health checks, and emergency revocation playbook.

Hiro — can you validate that our runtime can validate SAN URI fields the way Alex describes and add any limits on the accepted OID formats?

Diego — once we have Alex's confirmation on legacy device counts, I'll produce the final runbook and a short compliance exceptions worksheet.

Thanks,
Kimberly
Director, Security Engineering, Redwood Inference

We will include two example DNS layouts in the workshop:
1) SRV-first layout (clients that support SRV): _redwood-api._tcp.redbank.internal -> SRV entries -> targets (host:port)
2) Fallback layout for legacy devices: redbank-legacy.internal -> A + port documented; TTL short, monitored with alerts on mismatch.
